extractedText: Millions Are Now Waiting Longer To Claim Social Security - Here's WhyPaige CerulliSat, July 25, 2026 at 11:00 AM UTC0 Millions of retirees depend on Social Security senior benefits, but applicants are facing longer wait times for their claim appointments. The Social Security program has faced numerous challenges this year, including staffing losses, and the longer appointment wait times are creating a barrier for Americans who wish to begin claiming their benefits. Here are some of the factors behind the delays, details on the individuals the delays are hurting the most, and tips on how to best navigate signing up to claim your benefits. Find Out: 13 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about.Social Security claim appointment wait times are rising According to Social Security data, as of July 6, just 64.6% of initial claims were scheduled within 30 days. That figure is down from 78.1% a year earlier. The rate fell below 45% in some regions as long delays have become prevalent. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started.Why Social Security appointments are taking longer The delays in initial claim appointment scheduling come as the Social Security program struggles after the loss of about 7,800 employees. Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) cuts eliminated about 14% of the agency's workforce. The significant workforce reduction means fewer staff are available to schedule and host in-person and phone appointments, and slots available for initial claim appointments have also been reduced. Staffing shortages have also contributed to the temporary closure of some rural SSA offices, leaving beneficiaries with fewer options to seek help. SSA is testing a national scheduling system The Social Security Administration (SSA) is currently testing centralized national scheduling; if successful, the scheduling could replace the current system that requires beneficiaries to directly contact their local offices. The centralized national scheduling would distribute work to employees throughout the nation, and that distribution would be based on employees' skill set, knowledge, and availability. The system reportedly should streamline service, and it's being evaluated in Tennessee and Nevada. While the centralized system might have advantages, some SSA employees have expressed concern about the transition. In particular, there's concern about how to best address state-specific rules if claims are distributed nationally, rather than being sent to local offices which have a deep understanding of state rules. The SSA is actively encouraging beneficiaries to use the online portal, which is now available 24 hours a day. Beneficiaries may use the portal for numerous tasks, including checking payments, updating direct deposit information, and downloading benefit letters. What the SSA says about its customer service In June 2026, SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano told Congress that the agency is working to improve customer service, particularly by cutting the long wait times for the toll-free phone helpline. According to Bisignano, the average "speed of answer" had declined to the "lowest level in a decade," and in May the speed of answer was less than five minutes. Bisignano also highlighted technology upgrades being implemented, noting that such upgrades would save the agency the equivalent of 2,500 full-time employees. Additionally, the SSA is implementing automation for certain claims to help reduce wait times and serve more people faster. Who is most affected by the delays The delays in claim appointment scheduling may be financially harmful to certain beneficiaries who are most dependent on Social Security benefits. Since the claim appointment is the very beginning of the claim process, delays in scheduling that initial appointment push back when benefits actually begin. Since an average medical determination may take six to eight months for disability claims, delaying the process by another one to two months may create a financial hardship, leaving applicants to get by longer before receiving benefits. Older beneficiaries who are uncomfortable with online portals, disabled applicants, and low-income recipients face some of the steepest barriers created by these delayed appointments. Individuals who aren't comfortable with or can't afford technology may rely on phone or in-person customer service, which is increasingly difficult to access through the SSA. Such individuals are at risk because of these scheduling delays and customer service limitations.
